item.title: Emacs vs Neovim - Why Prot Won't Pick a Side
item.description:
youtube

After all my Neovim talk, Rumen brought @protesilaos (Prot) onto Root Access to balance things out, and Ted joined us too. Rumen shares that he converted to Emacs full time, is building a NixOS flavor, runs his tasks in Org mode, and is working on a small database server so the notes he dictates on his phone sync to Emacs on his desktop and laptop. We also get into the anti-AI "Human Emacs" fork idea, and Prot explains why Emacs already refuses LLM-generated contributions over copyright and GPL licensing concerns, and how maintainers spot suspicious patches. Prot says he doesn't use AI because programming is basically his video game, but he admits the technology case is undeniable and frames the AI bubble as a capital realignment like the dot-com crash. We also talk about how Cyprus and Greece export tourism and land, and the gold rush mentality that comes with it, and I ask Prot about Cypriot olive oil for my wife. Then it's Niri and scrolling window managers versus i3/Sway-style control, Emacs workspaces replacing tmux, and DHH's Omarchy, where Prot argues software should be judged on its merits and not its author, and explains why he refuses to remove a Modus theme port for Omarchy. I show Hazenbug's org mode plugin for Neovim, Prot explains why org is portable plain-text markup, and I explain why I'm not switching back to Emacs yet - I'm not on the Neovim team or the Emacs team, and editor choice shouldn't be treated like soccer or religion. If you care about Emacs, Neovim, free software, or how AI fits into all of it, this one is for you. Chai is an Emacs package for reading books in Org mode and keeping your notes where they belong. v2.1.0 is shown here with Thoreau's Walden. What's new in v2.1.0: • One right-click menu — every Chai action now lives in a single submenu • Mark while reading — highlight a line, say why, and the note stays inline next to it • Store the book — finished a book? Store all of its notes at once, then drop them into any Org note, with chapters and sources kept • Find it again — M-x chai-search searches every book at once; your marked passages rank first • Ask, with sources — M-x chai-ask asks your library a question (local LLM, e.g. qwen3.5:9b) and answers with citations you can follow back to the page

item.title: Emacs and rust on an ASUS Eee PC 1000HA
item.description:
youtube

In an effort to focus/mood setting, I am using these random devices for specific purposes eg. I use a black 2007 Macbook Pro to journal in and I'm using this one to learn rust in. Netbook info: - ASUS Eee PC 1000HA - Using Debian 12 - i686 arch The battery is shot and hard to find a good one to replace it with. I have 3 bad batteries from my attempts to get a good one. The one I use in this video can hold a charge for like 10 minutes so it's helpful. Installing emacs and rust - $sudo apt install rust - $sudo apt install emacs See screen at 2:41 for modifications in init.el file. My install did not come with an init.el file so I had to make it under /home/user/.emacs.d/init.el. The .emacs.d file is made automatically. As you make edits through the Emacs GUI eg. with M-x command settings are written to the init.el file. That's how I was able to get the theme to stick and later when installing rust-mode package to get syntax highlighting to work. I primarily had to use the Emacs GUI to get the theme installed/other situations addressed like the rust syntax highlighting. For rust don't use the curl/bash script method to install it, just stick with apt and then you'll have to bind the /usr/bin/rustc command to rustc if you want it to be easier to type. item.description:

🔴 LIVE Sun, Nov 8, 7:30 AM CST: Neovim + kitty Maintainers on AI, Terminal Security and What's Next | Justin M. Keyes & Kovid Goyal. Set a reminder: https://youtube.com/live/C0kQDam7PZs Why would someone leave Neovim for Emacs and stay there? In this clip, lucidlynx explains why everything in Neovim felt like a separate piece that never quite fit together, and why Emacs felt more integrated. I jump in with my own experience: I tried Emacs, I suffered, and I get what they mean about the Neovim ecosystem feeling like a puzzle of disconnected tools. We get into LunarVim disappearing, LazyVim's rapid-fire changes (like the move from nvim-cmp to blink.cmp breaking completion plugins), and how shell tools like EZA, BAT, ripgrep, FD, FZF and Zoxide never felt like part of a whole. lucidlynx also shares what the switch was actually like: remapping Caps Lock to Control, getting used to Emacs keybindings, and starting out with Doom Emacs. Later we talk about Emacs as a Lisp machine, using AI to port a VS Code plugin for HashiCorp Packer into Emacs, and why Org mode keeps coming up. If you're curious about Emacs, or tired of stitching your Neovim setup together, this one is worth a watch. item.title: grid-table — Runs Excel in Emacs
item.description:
youtube

grid-table (now rename to exc.el) is a spreadsheet for Emacs that behaves like Excel: the keys, the formulas, the error values and the file format. This tour uses one workbook, Northwind Tea Co., about 2,400 orders on three sheets, and shows what is new in 0.4. What you'll see: - The new view, drawn with ETAF, next to the old one - Excel keys: typing, RET, TAB, F2, fill, copy and paste with formats, undo - XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, FILTER, dynamic arrays that spill, LET and LAMBDA - One edit recalculates only what depends on it - Tracing where a number comes from, with error values that behave like Excel's - Floating charts over the cells - Results checked against Microsoft's own function examples - Export to .xlsx, edit in LibreOffice, open it again in Emacs - A workbook that reads another workbook's values - A new formula function in three lines of Lisp - Inside Org notes, and in a terminal Chapters: 0:00 Old view and new view, same edit 0:38 grid-table 0:49 Excel keys 1:34 Clean the orders 2:10 Look up and summarise 3:19 One edit, and only what depends on it 4:51 Make it presentable 5:25 Where did this number come from? 6:33 Names 8:00 Arrays that spill 9:50 LAMBDA 10:59 Text, dates and R1C1 13:15 A chart that floats 14:56 Checked against Excel 15:33 Send it to a colleague (.xlsx) 16:36 A workbook that reads another 17:36 Three lines of Lisp 18:08 In Org notes and in a terminal 18:32 Get it

item.title: Clutch: Query, Browse and Edit Databases Without Leaving Emacs
item.description:
youtube

Clutch is an Emacs package for querying and browsing databases, and for staging SQL row edits with a preview before anything runs. Results open in an interactive grid, and nothing is written until you review the exact SQL and confirm. Supported databases: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MongoDB and Redis natively, plus Oracle, SQL Server, ClickHouse, DuckDB and other databases through JDBC. In this demo we use PostgreSQL over its native protocol, then DuckDB over JDBC. Chapters 0:00 Connect and run a query 0:23 Foreign keys and NULL faces 0:32 Per-column displayers 0:57 Rectangle select and Refine 1:22 Aggregate and server-side filter 1:38 Stage, preview and submit an edit 1:59 Long JSON hover preview 2:35 Insert and delete rows 3:15 JDBC databases (DuckDB) What you will see - Run SQL in a normal buffer with C-c C-c - Foreign keys are underlined; NULL has its own face - Per-column displayers: turn raw values into colored labels - Rectangle selection (C-x SPC), then Refine (-r) to exclude rows and columns before copying as TSV, CSV or an Org table - Aggregate selected numeric cells, and filter with a server-side WHERE - Stage edits, preview the exact SQL (C-c C-p), then confirm - Long JSON hover preview (off by default: set clutch-cell-preview-style to child-frame) - Insert and delete rows through a form - JDBC: a Java 17+ agent runs beside Emacs; the same UI works over JDBC Install M-x package-install RET clutch Requirements: Emacs 29.1+. SQLite needs nothing else. Other native backends need their own Emacs package, and JDBC needs Java 17+. GitHub: https://github.com/LuciusChen/clutch MELPA: https://melpa.org/#/clutch ,#Emacs #SQL #Database
